lines.note: Gita completes Ico- at the end of f261, making Icogita fito, a person of the evasive kind just described. This is running text, whereas the repeated gita below f261's column is the catchword.
Icomeqi describes moving oneself in a particular manner. The Portuguese verb is Menearſe, not OCR Mencarſe; its specification of manner continues below.
Geito completes 'with a certain manner and bearing'. The ampersand links it to modo in the preceding row.

runs.text: Meter a ſeta, ou pilouro dẽ-

lines.note: Icomi means shooting an arrow or projectile into something. The initial is I, not OCR F; the Portuguese dẽ- begins dentro across the line division.

runs.text: tro de algũa couſa a que ſe tira.

lines.note: Tro completes dentro, specifying the object at which the shot is aimed. This describes penetration of the target, not loading a weapon.
Icon is inward resentment, explained by Vramiuo nocoſu, leaving a grievance behind. The weak middle strokes support m in Vramiuo rather than the OCR's ni sequence.
Magoa contra alguem completes the sense as hurt or grievance against someone. No new headword begins on this continuation.

runs.text: Çapatos tecidos, ou feitos de junco.

lines.note: Icongǒ denotes woven footwear made of rushes. The initial Portuguese Ç has a visible cedilla; the uncedilled OCR form is corrected.

runs.text: Experiencia que tem o medico de curar.

lines.note: Icot is the physician's experience in curing. The unfamiliar headword is retained without expanding its final t or forcing a modern term.

runs.text: Paßar por cima com ſeta, ou

lines.note: Icoxi means overshooting with an arrow or projectile. The scan reads Paßar rather than Pißar, and retains the source's historical oita principal part.

runs.text: pilouro, ou dar por cima do aluo, ou de outra

lines.note: The projectile goes above the target or above some other object. The Portuguese alternatives continue the same shooting sense.
Couſa a que ſe tira completes the object being aimed at. It closes Icoxi before the homophonous noun sequence begins.
Icqe here is a single flower, explained by Fito fana. The physical word separation in that Japanese phrase is retained.
The next Icqe is one house or family, with iye identifying the homophone. A capital I is visible at the headword's beginning.
This Icqei means one valley, explained by Fitotçuno tani. It is distinct from the view or scenery entry immediately below.
The second Icqei denotes a view or scene, with qei as its Japanese explanation. The missing initial I is restored; Excel- starts the Portuguese qualification on the next row.
Lente completes Excellente; the view is excellent and pleasing. The Portuguese gives the qualitative force of the preceding Japanese qei.
Icqen is illustrated by the past expression Icqen tçucamatçutta, taking a look. The gloss begins 'I gave' and continues below.

runs.text: hũa viſta, ou paßei hũa vez com os olhos.

lines.note: Completes Dei hũa viſta as taking a look or passing one's eyes over something once. The beta-like doubled-s form in paßei is retained.
This Icqen denotes one dog, explicitly equated with Inu ippiqi. The abraded c is consistent with neighboring Icqen forms, not OCR e.
A third Icqen is one fist, with cobuxi identifying the sense. The draft's initial le is corrected to the scan-supported Ic sequence.

Icqeô and icqiô are alternative forms introduced by Latin l. Both mean something singular or extraordinary; the scan supports the eô/iô pair and extraordinario, not the OCR's extra prefix or extreordinario.
Icqiôna xitacu illustrates distinctive attire or preparation, glossed Trajo ſingular. Item then begins another sense of the same word.

runs.text: Prazer, ou goſto dos que eſtão em algum a-

lines.note: The additional sense is the pleasure or enjoyment of people gathered together. The final a- begins ajuntamento below.
Juntamento completes ajuntamento. Icqiôuo moyouo- begins an example about stirring up enjoyment; q, rather than the OCR's e, is visible in the repeated headword.

runs.text: Excitar agente a algum particular pra-

lines.note: ſu completes moyouoſu. The gloss describes rousing the company to a particular pleasure, with prazer divided at the line end.
Zer completes prazer; aluoraçala further describes enlivening or exciting the company. The printed unaccented form is retained.
Icqet is a tied unit, explained as Ieni icquan, a thousand coins on a string. Ieni is the source's spelling of the money term; the damaged headword initial is restored as I.
Caxas enfiadas em hũa corda completes the specification of a thousand coins strung on one cord. The Japanese explanatory phrase above establishes the monetary context.
The next Icqet is a decision or settlement, explained by ſadame. Its initial is I, not the OCR's long-s/o sequence.
Determinação completes the alternative sense as a determination about something. The scan has a continuous word, not OCR deter minação.

runs.text: Hũa pauiola, ou ceſto de acarretar ter-

lines.note: This Icqi is a carrying basket or litter for moving earth. The initial I is restored; the Portuguese ter- continues as terra below.
Ra completes terra, the earth carried in the basket or litter; &c leaves its other loads unspecified.

runs.text: Aleuantamento, ou mutim de laur adores

lines.note: This Icqi denotes a cultivators' uprising. The first I is severely worn but faint residual ink and the repeated Icqiuo below support it; the printed internal gap in laur adores is retained.
The uprising is against their lord. Icqiuo vocoſu means raising such a revolt; A- begins its Portuguese explanation below.

runs.text: leuantarſe contra o ſenhor da terra.

lines.note: Leuantarſe completes Aleuantarſe, rising against the lord of the land. This closes the revolt sense rather than returning to the carrying-basket entry.
Icqicu means a handful, explained by Fito niguiri. The scan supports c in the headword and the faint t in Fito, correcting Ieqicu and Fio.
Chea completes mão chea, a full hand. Final S is the upright label for written usage.

Icqiǒ is one mirror, explained by cagami. The initial I is abraded at the same margin as adjacent entries; its remaining trace is compatible with this reading. This is a flush-left headword, not an indented continuation.
Icqi tǒjen describes a warrior worth a thousand. The scan supports the headword sequence Icqi, not OCR ſeqi; the weak vowel mark is retained as the draft's caron.

Pormil completes 'worth a thousand'; the Japanese example specifies such a warrior. The repeated tojeno is left unmarked because its o is very weak and no clear accent can be established; no accent is supplied merely from the headword above.
Icqiǔ is one rest or pause, explained by Fito yaſumi. The headword's capital I and marked u are retained; re- continues below.
Pouſo completes repouſo, the second rest gloss. Final S is an upright written-register label.
Icqua means one fault or sin, with toga supplying its Japanese explanation. The worn initial I is retained from compatible residual strokes, and final S is upright.
Icquacu means one crane, explicitly explained by Tçuru fitotçu. The scan supports the cq cluster rather than OCR aq, and the final usage label is upright.

runs.text: Hum ajuntamento de gente que ſe

lines.note: Icquai is a gathering of people. The headword's worn opening still supports Icquai rather than OCR tequai; the activities of the gathering follow below.

runs.text: ajũta pera folgar, fazer verſos, beber cha, & c.

lines.note: The company gathers to enjoy itself, compose verses, or drink tea. The verb is folgar, not OCR folgas, and the abbreviated nasal in ajũta is preserved.
This Icquai is one circuit or turn, explained by Fitomeguri. The c is visible rather than OCR e, and final S is the upright written-register label.

Icubi denotes a person with a short neck, made explicit by Cubino mijicai mono. The Portuguese peſ continues into coço below; the apparent final i in the draft is part of the rule, not another letter.
Coço completes peſcoço. The example Icubina fito repeats the short-necked-person sense; abrasion affects b and n, but their remaining strokes support this reading rather than Icub ira.
Icuchi is a kind of mushroom, as the Portuguese cugumelos states. No modern species identification is imposed.
Icudaqi means breaking or shattering something by shooting it. The instrumental Portuguese cõ leads into the arrow or projectile specified below.
ſeta, ou pilouro completes the means of breaking the object: an arrow or projectile. It belongs to Icudaqi, not a separate weapon entry.
Icufodomonǒ means in a short time, explained by Fodomo ſezu. The source supports f in the headword and long ſ in ſezu; breue is complete at the edge, not the draft's breu-.
Tempo, ou eſpaço completes 'in a short time or interval'. This is the continuation of breue, not a continuation of a divided word.
Icufodonǒ is given as an equivalent shorter form, with Idem referring back to the preceding short-time expression.

The native scan clearly prints Icurami, with mi before the comma, although the supplied NINJAL headword index lists Icura.; preserve the printed anomaly rather than emending it. Vouoqi coto expresses abundance. Enlarged comparison with quantidade below confirms n in Quantidade, not the draft's m; mul continues without an added hyphen.
Tidaõ completes the divided multitude term; the tilde is over the final o, not a grave accent. Icuramo aru illustrates there being a large quantity, with the Portuguese Auer continued below.
Muito em quantidade completes the abundance example. Item then introduces interrogative Icura?, asking an amount rather than asserting abundance.

runs.text: perguntar quanto val algũa couſa, ou por quã

lines.note: The explanation specifies asking what something is worth or the price for which it was bought. The nasal abbreviation in quã is retained at the right edge.
To completes quanto. Icurani vocaiattaca? is the respectful price question, with the historical vocaiattaca retained rather than modernized.
The Portuguese translates the question as 'For how much did you buy it?' The abbreviation in cõpraſtes remains unexpanded.
Icuſa means war or battle. The source retains l in batalha and repeats Icuſauo, not OCR Izuſauo; the example's verb follows on the next row.

runs.text: Ceßar de pelejar, ou deixar aguerra.

lines.note: Yamuru completes Icuſauo yamuru, stopping fighting or leaving war. The historical verbal ending is retained, as is the printed aguerra spacing.
Icuſauo ſuru means making war or fighting. The Portuguese bata- continues onto the next row.
Lhar completes batalhar. Icuſauo xicaquru introduces beginning or launching hostilities against another, with guerra itself divided here.

runs.text: ra a outro, ou começar a fazer guerra.

lines.note: Ra completes guerra and the gloss specifies attacking another or beginning to wage war. It explains the causative or initiating force of xicaquru.
Icuſauo tomuru means stopping or preventing warfare. The Portuguese fazer continues into the infinitive below.
Ceßar aguerra completes 'make the war cease'. The beta-like doubled-s type and the printed joined aguerra are preserved.
Icuſaba is the battlefield. The Portuguese has initial b in batalha, not OCR h; both languages identify the place of fighting.
Icuſa buguiǒ is a military officer, compared in the gloss to a field commander or sergeant. The Portuguese rank comparison is retained without imposing a modern equivalence.
Icuſadate concerns military ordering, disposition, or arrangement. The objects arranged are supplied by the continuation below.

runs.text: do arrayal, ou gente de guerra.

lines.note: The arrangement is of the camp or the fighting force. This completes the military sense of Icuſadate.
Icuſagami is the deity of war, compared to Mars. Cami is the Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is treated separately from the surrounding italic text.
Icuſama asks 'in how many ways?' The u in Icu- is visible rather than the OCR's o, linking it to the following interrogative forms.
Icutabi asks how many times. The noun or counter for occurrences contrasts with the person-counting form below.
Icutari asks how many people. The Portuguese peßoas makes the human counting sense explicit.
Icutçu is the general 'how many?' form, glossed with both Portuguese grammatical genders. Its first letter is capital I, not a long s.

runs.text: Hum certo peixe de rio como mugem.

lines.note: IDa names a river fish compared with mugem. The large I belongs to this headword and spans two rows; it was omitted from the draft and is restored with enlarged-initial metadata.
Idaqedacani describes a stiff, elevated bodily posture. It is a new headword displaced rightward by the preceding enlarged I, not a continuation of the fish entry.

runs.text: hirto, & aleuãtado com o corpo Vt,

lines.note: The gloss describes holding the body erect and raised. Ida- begins the example, retaining the source's lack of punctuation after corpo.
Qedacani completes Idaqedacani, followed by natte iru, remaining in that posture. The Portuguese reads poſtura with u, not OCR poſtara.
Do corpo completes the explanation as a posture of the body. This short continuation closes the adverbial entry.
Idaqi means embracing or holding in one's arms. The principal parts and Portuguese Abraçar agree on the action.
Idaqiague means taking or raising something in one's arms. The object phrase nos continues below.
Braços completes nos braços, specifying the arms in which something is lifted or held.
Idaqiai is mutual embracing. The faint initial I is restored and the uǒ principal parts are retained as printed.
Idaqiſodate means raising a child while carrying it in one's arms. The headword begins with a worn capital I and retains long ſ in the sodate element.
The example Couo idaqi ſodatçuru specifies raising a child in one's arms. The damaged consonant is d, not the second o of OCR ſooatçuru, consistent with the headword and its Portuguese gloss.
Idaqitçuqi means embracing or clinging to someone. The Portuguese supplies alguem as the person embraced.
Idaqitori means taking someone or something into one's arms. The scan's worn initial is capital I, and the otta principal part is preserved.

runs.text: Cozerſe a couſa bem que ſe poſ

lines.note: Idari describes food becoming thoroughly cooked. The scan supports Idari, not OCR Auari; the final poſ continues into ſa on the next row without an added hyphen.
ſa completes poſſa, so the food is cooked enough to be eaten. The separate far-right idaxi is a catchword anticipating f263 and is moved out of the body under its own ID.
